terms.definition: A system in which rewards and positions go to people on the basis of ability and effort rather than background.
terms.examiner: Functionalists (Davis and Moore, Parsons) claim education is meritocratic; Marxists call this the myth of meritocracy. Say whose view you are giving.

terms.definition: The sense of belonging and shared values that binds members of a society together.
terms.examiner: Durkheim's term: education passes on a shared culture, for example through history lessons. Link it to the 'specialist skills' function for a second point.

terms.definition: Rules and judgements applied equally to everyone, such as the same exams and school rules for all pupils.
terms.examiner: Parsons contrasts them with the particularistic standards of the family. A clear contrast with the family earns the application marks.

terms.definition: The sifting and sorting of people into the jobs best suited to their abilities.
terms.examiner: Davis and Moore's function of education. Evaluate with evidence that class, not ability, still predicts outcomes.

terms.definition: The knowledge and skills of the workforce, seen by neoliberals as a source of economic growth.
terms.examiner: The New Right and neoliberal view of what schools are for; useful to link to marketisation and vocational policies.

terms.definition: Institutions that control people by shaping their ideas rather than by force; Althusser includes education.
terms.examiner: Althusser says education reproduces class inequality and legitimates it. Contrast with the repressive state apparatus (police, courts).

terms.definition: The idea that the relationships and rules of school mirror those of the capitalist workplace.
terms.examiner: Bowles and Gintis. Give an example of a parallel, such as obeying teachers and obeying managers, rather than just naming the principle.

terms.definition: The lessons pupils learn from the way school is organised, such as obedience, punctuality and accepting hierarchy, without being formally taught.
terms.examiner: Do not confuse it with the formal curriculum. Marxists and feminists use it in different ways: say which you mean.

terms.definition: The Marxist claim that education only appears to reward merit, so that inequality looks fair.
terms.examiner: Bowles and Gintis. Pair it with evidence that middle-class pupils get better results at the same ability level.

terms.definition: Willis's study of twelve working-class 'lads' whose counter-school culture led them into manual jobs.
terms.examiner: Shows that pupils are not passive, which challenges Bowles and Gintis's correspondence theory: good evaluation material.

terms.definition: The view that the state should do less and markets should do more, including in public services such as education.
terms.examiner: Often paired with the New Right. Link it to competition between schools and to the human capital idea.

terms.definition: The passing on of class inequality from one generation to the next.
terms.examiner: The core Marxist claim about education. State who is reproduced and how, for example through cultural capital (Bourdieu).
